extracted.intended_audience: magazine readers interested in comedy and pop culture
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for assessing a shock-driven stand-up comedian's material, stagecraft, ethics, and commercial impact, illustrated by a profile of Sam Kinison. Focuses on what makes provocative comedy effective, how audiences respond, and where moral or commercial lines are drawn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature vocal/physical gimmick
rubrics_metrics.description: The unearthly scream — "a supersonic boom born of bile" — functions as the comedian's calling card.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scream converts the room and defines Kinison's act; physical bits (pant mime gun, on-knees imitations) amplify jokes. Examples: his scream onstage and pantomime shootings that elicit crowd reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage presence and charisma
rubrics_metrics.description: Daunting charisma and imposing physical presence that dominate the stage while also containing contradictory characteristics (e.g., 'Muppet-like cuteness').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence allows performance to sell large venues and sustain attention despite controversial material. The profile notes his ability to play 5000-seat arenas and pull off otherwise offensive material because of charisma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief and commitment to persona
rubrics_metrics.description: The preacher’s ability to 'believe what he wants to believe — no matter how wrongheaded — and make others act accordingly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conviction animates material and can persuade or galvanize audiences (anecdote: Kinison believing the insurance-policy story and turning it into rage). Anti-pattern: acting without accurate information but with full conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outrageousness and shock value as a tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Raiding taboos (televangelists, sobriety, women, gays, religious imagery) and escalating nastiness to generate publicity and audience energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shock helps generate press and notoriety (SNL, controversial bits, video). But the article warns that escalating for its own sake ('being naughty for naughtiness' sake') can be dubious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral responsibility and potential for societal harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Preaching a 'gospel of irresponsibility' can raise serious moral questions about whether audiences are entertained or being led toward harmful attitudes or actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the 'Rubber Love' routine accused of gay-baiting and misleading audiences about AIDS; fans dismissing AIDS hotline cards. The metric weighs ethical consequences and social impact of jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual accuracy versus comedic license
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedian's defense: 'They say my jokes aren’t medically correct. They don’t have to be. They’re not prescriptions, they’re fucking jokes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While comedy need not be factually accurate, the article shows real-world consequences (label employees petitioning, Warner Bros inserting AIDS info). Evaluate whether inaccuracies are acceptable given potential harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience composition and immediate reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: The demographic makeup and live response (e.g., 'seventy-five percent male, mostly in its twenties — cheers and stomps') as a measure of effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience uptake (cheers, stomps, leaving behavior) indicates resonance; examples include fans dropping hotline cards or screaming on exit — showing emotional impact but also possible misreading of serious issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success and marketing instincts
rubrics_metrics.description: Sales, venue size, and savvy promotional moves as measures of a comedian's success (albums selling, gold records, rock-pricing venues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites 100,000 album sales for Louder Than Hell, current album going gold, and Kinison playing 5000-seat venues — showing that controversy plus branding can yield commercial results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-genre branding and celebrity alliances
rubrics_metrics.description: Aligning with other cultural figures (heavy-metal musicians, celebrities) and music-video tactics to amplify reach and create an image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a heavy-metal cover of 'Wild Thing', video cameo appearances by Billy Idol and members of popular bands, and tabloid links (Jessica Hahn) that fuel visibility and sell the persona.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity stunts and theatrical antics
rubrics_metrics.description: Performative stunts (breaking a stool, mock crucifixion with ketchup, provocative video scenes) used to generate attention and cultivate a rebellious image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stunts have concrete effects: club suspensions, riots, sold-out returns, and tabloid coverage. Evaluate whether stunts build a sustainable career or simply create short-term notoriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship with censorship and gatekeepers
rubrics_metrics.description: How a comedian navigates editorial limits and censorship (e.g., ignoring SNL censors, demanding more stage time) to maximize exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kinison ignored censors on SNL but parlayed the controversy into hosting the show later. Consider risks and rewards of defying platforms versus working within them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal vulnerability and backstory adding depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal tragedy or vulnerability (the article notes Kinison 'seems devastated by the suicide of his brother Kevin') that complicates or deepens a shock-based persona.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depth can humanize an otherwise abrasive persona and affect audience sympathy. Use personal history to assess complexity beyond surface outrage.
